title: Reads vs writes
summary: Read replicas scale reads; the primary handles writes.

lesson.problem: Even with a cache, the database is busy. Most of the traffic is reads, and the writes are stuck waiting behind them.
why: Typical applications read far more than they write, often 10 to 100 reads for every write. A single primary database accepts all writes and streams the changes to read replicas.
App servers send writes to the primary and spread reads across the replicas, so read capacity grows by adding replicas.
Replication is usually asynchronous, so a replica can be a little behind the primary (replication lag).
takeaways: Replicas scale reads, not writes. Scaling writes needs sharding.
Replication lag breaks read-your-own-writes: read from the primary right after a user changes something.
If the primary fails, a replica can be promoted, which also makes replicas a high-availability tool.
